summary: REJECT. V2 repairs the fabricated D-015 routing, self-granted-disposition posture, source must-not citation, historical coordinator pin, and closed lineage roster. It chooses no SDK API, mints no D9/exit or D-096 (A) grant, and makes no SATISFIED, QUALIFIED, or implementation claim. The central cancellation repair still fails. CSCV2-B1 finds no executable transition relation: deadline and post-death triggers cannot be represented consistently by the applied provider contract, eligibility has no evaluation point or teardown fence, terminal/failure branches are absent, and G20 has no trace oracle. CSCV2-B2 finds that noFanoutWhen expressly permits provider-to-supervision translation 'except under' J-1 even though J-1 is byte-opaque and orders only an independently issued CPC cancel against provider-result arrival. At 2 blockers and 0 SHOULD-FIX, DR-125 remains OPEN and this verdict authorizes nothing.

blockers.title: The claimed fanout is not a valid composed transition relation
blockers.measurement: V2 adds a trigger list and says both carriers happen IFF the applied provider protocol has a live in-band Cancel transition, but it does not define when liveness is sampled, how the two sends are ordered or fenced, what happens when the in-band write fails, or how terminal/fault states branch. Two newly listed triggers are incompatible with the measured applied surfaces. TypeScript CancelV1.reason is closed to user-interrupt|host-shutdown and its supervision.userCancellation trigger is SIGINT/SIGTERM; no deadline reason or deadline-to-host-shutdown mapping exists. Its Cancel may be sent once from a nonterminal state. CPC J-3 makes process death the LAST merged event after every channel is drained, so an observed death cannot initiate an in-band transition; TypeScript additionally treats a signal death not caused by prior host cancellation as provider-protocol fault, while a death caused by prior user cancellation follows an already-sent Cancel and must not trigger a second one. The unchanged G20 text names the two carriers but supplies no cause/order/terminal oracle.
counterexamples: A host-owned deadline expires while TypeScript is nonterminal. The state admits a Cancel frame, but the closed payload has no deadline reason. Sending user-interrupt or host-shutdown invents a cause mapping; omitting the frame contradicts dualCarrierFanoutRequiredWhen plus 'Both happen.'

The host emits CPC supervision cancel first; the component exits on the teardown announcement before the provider-side participant writes Cancel. If 'live' is evaluated after that exit, the IFF silently suppresses the in-band path; if it is evaluated at the trigger, the required transition is now impossible. V2 defines neither evaluation point nor a fence.

A user cancellation already sent the one permitted provider Cancel and forced cleanup later yields process death. Treating the observed death as another required fanout either sends a forbidden second Cancel or cannot satisfy 'Both happen.'
blockers.whyBlocker: The core Codex-v1 blocker required a behavioral composition that preserves reachability of the applied provider transition and defines terminal/fault branches. Naming causes plus an eventual 'both' assertion does not make the transition executable, and the added deadline/death causes create contradictions with the very applied contracts the IFF is supposed to preserve. The central T-1 repair therefore remains incomplete.
blockers.requiredRepair: Define the fanout as an explicit host-event transition relation, conditional on the owning provider contract's admissible cause and current state. Sample eligibility at a named point; commit the provider-side in-band transition before any CPC teardown action that can preclude it, or specify an equivalent atomic barrier; define write-failure, already-terminal, already-cancelled, no-in-band-cancel, deadline, and process-death branches without fabricating provider payload reasons. Process death must be an observation/terminal branch, not a post-death send trigger. Add G20 traces with determinate expected carrier order and outcomes. Do not mint an SDK API, provider frame, D9/exit, or D-096 (A) grant.

blockers.title: The no-fanout clause invents a J-1 exception to the no-translation boundary
blockers.measurement: noFanoutWhen says the control plane does not translate a provider-only in-band Cancel into supervision meaning 'except under the owning J-1 join.' CPC J-1 supplies no such exception: its cancel-issued event is the CPC control frame, and it orders that control event against a provider result final-octet boundary. CPC's merged-order mechanism exposes provider boundary facts only, never content, and leaves meaning to the owning provider contract. The candidate's sibling mustNot sentence correctly says the control plane cannot translate provider meaning to resolve a race. The 'except' clause therefore both contradicts the candidate and silently widens J-1/DR-102.
blockers.counterexample: For a provider-side in-band Cancel that is not independently a host control cancellation, an implementation can cite the exception to derive CPC teardown/supervision meaning from the provider semantic frame. That is precisely the semantic bridge file 02 and CPC forbid; alternatively, if J-1 remains byte-opaque as written, the exception is unreachable and the proposed no-fanout behavior has no defined join at all.
blockers.whyBlocker: This is an explicit authorization inside the core T-1 composition, not editorial ambiguity. It permits the control plane to infer supervision from provider semantics under a join that only binds ordering, contradicting the no-translation rule and the candidate's claim not to rewrite DR-102.
blockers.requiredRepair: Remove the exception. State that a provider-side in-band Cancel with no independently host-owned control-cancellation event remains wholly within the provider contract and never creates CPC supervision meaning. Clarify that J-1 orders an independently emitted CPC cancel against provider-result boundary events only; it neither observes nor translates an in-band Cancel.
